guide.room: Tiny Eye (a house drawn, a neuron card open)
guide.question: What does this neuron do?
guide.answer: Neuron ninety-nine responds most to simple houses with peaked roofs, and also to castles. A bigger A I named it that and, from the name alone, picked four out of four hidden doodles from its strongest examples; that’s good evidence for the job, though the card only suggests what it does.
problems: Leaves out the 'fires least' end shown on the card: small rounded shapes with loose curved lines, which only passed 2 of 4 so it is a fuzzier description.
Doesn't mention that for this drawing the neuron is firing extremely strongly (higher than 100 of 100 sample doodles), which helps answer what it is doing now.
Says 'responds most to simple houses with peaked roofs, and also to castles' but doesn't clearly tie this to the class bars / compared-with-all-samples numbers on the card.

guide.room: Tiny Eye (a house drawn, a neuron card open)
guide.question: Why did it guess that?
guide.answer: It saw a tiny, twenty-eight-by-twenty-eight picture, and house was its strongest guess at ninety percent. Neuron ninety-nine fires especially strongly for peaked-roof houses, so it may have helped; switching off busy neurons and watching the guess change can test which ones mattered.
problems: Does not mention that the model only knows 24 kinds and must always pick one, which was part of the needed explanation.
Says 'neuron ninety-nine' may have helped, but box three only shows one neuron card; the stronger grounding is that many neurons light up and vote together.
Mostly grounded and accurate otherwise: house is 90%, it sees 28×28 dots, and switching neurons off can test which mattered.

guide.room: Tiny Eye (a house drawn, a neuron card open)
guide.question: Do bigger eyes have cleaner neurons?
guide.answer: No. Tests of three eye sizes found their neurons were about equally clean, so a bigger eye didn’t make cleaner neurons.

guide.room: Tiny Eye (a house drawn, a neuron card open)
guide.question: What happens if I switch off a neuron?
guide.answer: That tiny part of the eye goes quiet, and its output becomes zero. The guess may change or stay the same; you can try the switch on this neuron’s card or in “switch neurons off.”

guide.room: Tiny Eye (a house drawn, a neuron card open)
guide.question: Why do the other kinds say under 1% instead of 0%?
guide.answer: Its teachers trained it never to be completely sure: even the right answer counted as about ninety percent, with the rest shared among the other kinds. So each kind keeps a tiny sliver; for this drawing, all the other nineteen kinds together add up to seven percent.

guide.room: Tiny Eye (scrubbed back to step 1,206, neuron 117's growth story open)
guide.question: Is the eye finished learning here?
guide.answer: No. This is step one thousand two hundred and six of nine thousand three hundred and sixty, so the eye is still learning; its neurons’ jobs are only about twenty percent settled, and it gets more doodles right later in training.

guide.room: Tiny Eye (scrubbed back to step 1,206, neuron 117's growth story open)
guide.question: How did this neuron grow?
guide.answer: Neuron one hundred seventeen began as a house-roof neuron around step six hundred. As training continued, peaked umbrellas joined its favorites; by the end, they made up about a fifth of its top hundred doodles, just below houses.

guide.question: What changed when I squeezed it?
guide.answer: The squeezed eye has just eight last-stage neurons instead of two hundred and fifty-six, so each has to cover more kinds of things: four point one on average, compared with three point three in the full eye. Its neurons are broader, not muddled, and its accuracy is a little lower: eighty-four out of a hundred instead of eighty-eight.

guide.question: Why does this neuron like rainbows and umbrellas?
guide.answer: Rainbows, umbrellas, and some castles have curved, upside-down U shapes. This neuron seems to notice those shapes, though its card only gives us a clue about its job.
